questions.text: Walk me through the most technically complex system you have built or significantly changed. What made it hard, and what did you personally contribute?
questions.rationale: Separates genuine depth from proximity to someone else's work; the follow-up pressure is on personal contribution.

questions.text: Tell me about a bug that took you days to find. How did you finally track it down?
questions.rationale: Reveals debugging methodology and persistence rather than tool familiarity alone.

questions.text: Describe a time you had to make a tradeoff between shipping quickly and doing it right. What did you choose and why?
questions.rationale: Probes engineering judgment under real constraints, the daily texture of the job.

questions.text: How do you decide when code needs a comment?
questions.rationale: A small question that reliably exposes how a candidate thinks about future readers.

questions.text: Tell me about a code review where you and the author disagreed. How was it resolved?
questions.rationale: Screens for how a candidate handles technical disagreement with a peer.

questions.text: Describe a production incident you were involved in. What was your role during and after?
questions.rationale: Behavior during incidents shows composure, ownership, and blameless postmortem instincts.

questions.text: What is a piece of technology you were excited about that did not live up to it? What changed your mind?
questions.rationale: Tests intellectual honesty and whether enthusiasm is paired with evaluation.

questions.text: Walk me through how you would design a rate limiter for a public API.
questions.rationale: A bounded design exercise that reveals systems thinking without requiring a whiteboard marathon.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you inherited someone else's code that you found difficult. What did you do?
questions.rationale: Most engineering work is brownfield; this screens for pragmatism over rewrite instinct.

questions.text: How do you approach writing tests? What do you test first and what do you skip?
questions.rationale: Elicits a real testing philosophy rather than a yes to the question of whether they test.

questions.text: Describe a time you pushed back on a product requirement for technical reasons. What happened?
questions.rationale: Screens for constructive pushback and cross-functional communication rather than silent compliance.

questions.text: What part of software engineering do you find genuinely fun, and what part do you tolerate?
questions.rationale: Honest self-knowledge about energy sources predicts fit for the actual work mix.

questions.text: Tell me about the best engineering team you have been part of. What made it work?
questions.rationale: Reveals what team behaviors the candidate values and will try to reproduce.

questions.text: Describe a time you had to learn a new language or framework under deadline. How did you approach it?
questions.rationale: Learning velocity under pressure matters more than current stack overlap.

questions.text: How would you explain a race condition to a non-technical stakeholder whose feature is delayed by one?
questions.rationale: Tests whether understanding is deep enough to translate without jargon.

questions.text: Tell me about a technical decision you made that you later reversed. What triggered the reversal?
questions.rationale: Willingness to reverse a decision under evidence is a strong signal against ego-driven architecture.

questions.text: What does code ownership mean to you on a shared codebase?
questions.rationale: Screens for collaborative ownership norms versus territorial behavior.

questions.text: Describe your experience with database schema design. Walk me through a schema you designed and one thing you would change about it now.
questions.rationale: Pairs a depth probe with a self-criticism probe; strong candidates always have the second half.

questions.text: Why engineering, and why now at this kind of company?
questions.rationale: Distinguishes deliberate career intent from default drift.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you shipped something you were not proud of. What were the circumstances?
questions.rationale: Tests candor and how the candidate reasons about acceptable compromise.

questions.text: How do you keep a pull request reviewable? What is your personal size or scope limit?
questions.rationale: A concrete habit question that separates practiced collaborators from lone wolves.

questions.text: Describe a system you monitored in production. What signals did you watch and which one saved you at least once?
questions.rationale: Real operational experience produces specific answers; theory produces generic dashboards.

questions.text: Tell me about a time a senior engineer disagreed with your approach and turned out to be wrong. How did you handle it?
questions.rationale: Screens for spine paired with respect, especially important for early-career hires.

questions.text: What would you do in your first month to become productive in a codebase of two hundred thousand lines?
questions.rationale: Reveals a concrete onboarding strategy: reading, tracing, asking, shipping something small.

questions.text: Walk me through how you profile and fix a slow endpoint.
questions.rationale: Performance work has a method; this checks the candidate has one.

questions.text: Describe a time you mentored a junior engineer. What did you focus on and how did they grow?
questions.rationale: Leads multiply the team; specific mentoring stories evidence that instinct.

questions.text: Tell me about a project where requirements changed significantly midway. How did you and the team adapt?
questions.rationale: Change tolerance and re-planning behavior, screened through a real story.

questions.text: What is your approach when you estimate a task at two days and on day three it is still not done?
questions.rationale: Screens for early communication over silent heroics.

questions.text: As a tech lead, how do you split your attention between writing code and enabling the team? Give an example week.
questions.rationale: The concrete example week exposes whether the candidate has actually operated as a lead.

questions.text: What kind of engineering problem would make you take a pay cut to work on? Why that one?
questions.rationale: Locates genuine intrinsic motivation, which predicts retention on hard problems.
